orange-free-state.t: The Boer republic between the Orange and Vaal rivers, admired for its stable constitution, which fell with its ally the Transvaal in 1902.
orange-free-state.o: When Britain gave up the Orange River Sovereignty, the Bloemfontein Convention of 23 February 1854 recognised the burghers' independence. They adopted a constitution with an elected president and Volksraad and kept Bloemfontein as their capital.
orange-free-state.r: Citizenship was limited to white men, but the state gained a reputation for orderly government, especially under President Johannes Brand from 1864 to 1888. Wars with the Basotho Kingdom won fertile land in the Caledon valley. Britain's seizure of the diamond fields of Griqualand West was settled with a payment of £90,000 in 1876. Farming of sheep and grain dominated the economy.
orange-free-state.e: Under President Martinus Theunis Steyn the Free State joined the South African Republic against Britain in 1899. Britain annexed it in 1900, and the 1902 Treaty of Vereeniging confirmed it as the Orange River Colony.

odessos.t: Milesian colony on the Bay of Varna that linked Thracian kingdoms to Aegean trade for five centuries and grew into modern Varna.
odessos.o: Odessos was founded by colonists from Miletus on the western Black Sea coast, usually dated to c. 585-570 BCE, at the mouth of a valley leading inland towards Thrace. The site had good anchorage and access to fertile land, and the colony grew through exchange with the Thracian Getae and Odrysians of the interior.
odessos.r: Odessos was a self-governing Greek polis whose prosperity rested on grain, fish, wine imports and trade with Thracian rulers, whose wealth appears in rich local tombs. Its chief deity was the Great God, a Hellenised form of the Thracian Darzalas, shown on its coins. Under Lysimachus it joined a revolt of the Pontic cities in 313 BCE.
odessos.e: Like Tomis, Callatis and Mesembria, Odessos came under Roman control after the campaign of Marcus Terentius Varro Lucullus in 72-71 BCE. As Odessus it prospered in the Roman province of Moesia, with large public baths, and later passed to Byzantium and the Bulgarians. The modern city is Varna.
odessos.re: Ancient Greek religion (cult of the Great God)

old-kingdom-of-egypt.t: Egypt of the Third to Sixth Dynasties, the age of the pyramids and of an all-powerful god-king ruling from Memphis.
old-kingdom-of-egypt.o: The Old Kingdom began around 2686 BCE with the Third Dynasty, which followed Early Dynastic Egypt. Its king Djoser and his official Imhotep built the Step Pyramid at Saqqara, the first monumental stone building, and the kings of the Fourth Dynasty turned the experiment into true pyramids.
old-kingdom-of-egypt.r: Sneferu built the pyramids at Dahshur and Meidum, and his son Khufu raised the Great Pyramid at Giza, followed by Khafre and Menkaure. A literate bureaucracy headed by the vizier taxed grain and organised labour on a vast scale. The Fifth Dynasty favoured the sun god Ra with sun temples, and Unas had the Pyramid Texts carved in his tomb. Expeditions sought turquoise in Sinai and incense in Punt.
old-kingdom-of-egypt.e: Under the Sixth Dynasty, provincial governors (nomarchs) grew powerful and hereditary, and the very long reign of Pepi II was followed by weakness, possibly worsened by low Nile floods. Central authority faded around 2181 BCE, leaving the short-lived Eighth Dynasty of Egypt and the First Intermediate Period.

old-great-bulgaria.t: Khan Kubrat's short-lived Bulgar state north of the Black Sea, whose break-up sent Bulgars to the Danube and the Volga.
old-great-bulgaria.o: In the 630s Kubrat of the Dulo clan threw off the overlordship of the Avars and united the Onogur and Bulgar tribes of the steppe between the Kuban and the lower Dnieper. Raised partly at the court of Constantinople and baptised there, he made an alliance with the emperor Heraclius, who gave him the title of patrician.
old-great-bulgaria.r: Great Bulgaria was a confederation of Turkic-speaking nomadic tribes ruled by a khan of the Dulo clan, with Phanagoria on the Taman peninsula as a centre. Its wealth is shown by the treasure of Malaya Pereshchepina in Ukraine, often identified as Kubrat's burial, with gold and silver vessels and Byzantine gifts.
old-great-bulgaria.e: After Kubrat died around 665, his sons divided the people as Khazar pressure grew. Batbayan stayed and submitted to the Khazars, Kotrag led his followers north to found Volga Bulgaria, and Asparukh moved to the Danube, where he founded the First Bulgarian Empire in 681.

olbia-pontica.t: The leading Greek city on the northern Black Sea coast, a trading gateway between the Mediterranean world and the Scythian steppe.
olbia-pontica.o: Colonists from Miletus founded Olbia, meaning 'prosperous', around 550 BCE on the estuary of the Southern Bug, near an older Greek trading post on Berezan island. The site, close to the mouth of the Dnieper, gave access to the grain lands and river routes of Scythia.
olbia-pontica.r: Olbia was a democratic polis with an assembly, council and annual magistrates, and it cast distinctive bronze coins shaped like dolphins. Its merchants exported grain, fish and slaves and imported wine, oil and luxury goods. Herodotus visited the city, and his story of the Scythian king Scyles, who secretly lived as a Greek there, shows how closely the two worlds mixed.
olbia-pontica.e: Olbia resisted a siege by Alexander's general Zopyrion in 331 BCE but was badly sacked by the Getae around 55 BCE. Rebuilt on a smaller scale, it came under Roman protection in the 2nd century CE. Gothic attacks in the 3rd century and the Hunnic invasion in the 4th brought urban life to an end.

osroene.t: Osroene, the kingdom of Edessa in upper Mesopotamia, cradle of Syriac literature and one of the earliest centres of Christianity.
osroene.o: As the Seleucid Empire lost its eastern lands, a local dynasty of Arab origin took power at Edessa, modern Şanlıurfa, c. 132 BCE. Its kings, many called Abgar or Ma'nu, ruled a small kingdom between the Euphrates and Khabur, balancing Rome and the Parthian Empire.
osroene.r: Edessa grew rich on the trade crossing the Euphrates. Its kings wrote in Syriac, an Aramaic dialect that became a great literary language. A legend told of King Abgar V corresponding with Jesus, and Christianity spread early; Abgar VIII is often said to have converted, though this is debated.
osroene.e: Caracalla deposed the king in 214 CE and made Osroene a Roman colony. The dynasty was briefly restored but ended under Abgar X in the 240s, and the kingdom became a Roman province.

opuntian-locris.t: Confederation of the eastern Locrians on the Euboean Gulf, centred on Opus and remembered for the Locrian maidens sent to Troy.
opuntian-locris.o: The eastern Locrians lived along the coast of central Greece facing Euboea, separated from their western kin in Ozolian Locris by Doris and Phocis. Homer placed Ajax the Lesser among them. By the Archaic period their towns formed a confederation led by Opus, governed by an oligarchic council of a thousand.
opuntian-locris.r: The Locrians kept old customs, such as sending two noble maidens each year to serve Athena at Ilion in atonement for Ajax's sacrilege. An early 5th century BCE bronze tablet records the terms for Locrian colonists at Naupactus. They fought with Leonidas at Thermopylae in 480 BCE, then were forced to join the Persians, and later usually sided with Thebes and Sparta against Athens.
opuntian-locris.e: The Phocian League overran much of the region in the Third Sacred War. Eastern Locris later passed under Macedonian, Boeotian and Aetolian League control and came under Rome in 146 BCE.

oghuz-yabgu-state.t: The Oghuz Turkic state of the lower Syr Darya and Aral steppe, cradle of the Seljuks and of the Turkmen.
oghuz-yabgu-state.o: The Oghuz tribes moved from the eastern steppe to the lower Syr Darya and the Aral region in the 8th century, after the fall of the Western Turkic Khaganate and wars with the Karluks. By the 9th century they formed a confederation led by a ruler with the title yabghu.
oghuz-yabgu-state.r: The yabghu ruled from Yangikent near the mouth of the Syr Darya, a winter capital among nomadic pastures. The traveller Ibn Fadlan, who crossed their lands in 922, described their customs, military leaders and lack of Islam. They traded with Khwarazm and the Samanid Empire, and fought the Pechenegs and the Khazars. Islam spread among them in the 10th century.
oghuz-yabgu-state.e: Internal splits weakened the state; the Seljuk clan broke away to the south and conquered Iran from 1037. Around the mid-11th century the remaining Oghuz were pushed west by the Kipchaks of the Kimek Khanate, some becoming the Torks of the Russian steppe, others the Turkmen.

olba.t: Olba, a priestly principality in the hills of Rough Cilicia, ruled by high priests of Zeus who claimed descent from the hero Teucer.
olba.o: Olba grew around the sanctuary of Zeus Olbios at Uzuncaburç, in the mountains above the Cilician coast. In the Seleucid period it was governed by a line of high priests, the Teucrids, who traced their descent to Teucer, a hero of the Trojan War, and ruled the surrounding temple lands.
olba.r: The priest-kings controlled a territory of villages and forests from fortified towers. The temple of Zeus, built in the 3rd century BCE, still stands among later ruins. In the 1st century BCE the dynasty was disrupted by usurpers such as Zenophanes, whose daughter Aba won Roman favour.
olba.e: Under Augustus the Teucrid Ajax son of Teucer ruled as high priest and toparch. Polemon II of Pontus later held Olba, and Vespasian absorbed it into Roman Cilicia in 72 CE; the sanctuary town became Diocaesarea.

orlam-afrikaner-state.t: Jonker Afrikaner's horse-riding, gun-using Oorlam state that dominated central Namibia and founded Windhoek.
orlam-afrikaner-state.o: The Afrikaners were an Oorlam group, Khoekhoe of the Cape frontier who had adopted horses, guns and Cape Dutch, led by Jager Afrikaner. Around 1823 his son Jonker Afrikaner moved north at the invitation of the Nama to help them against the Herero, and by about 1840 he had settled at Windhoek, which he made his capital.
orlam-afrikaner-state.r: Jonker's mounted gunmen raided Herero cattle and controlled trade routes to Walvis Bay, where cattle were exchanged for guns, horses and brandy. He welcomed Wesleyan and Rhenish missionaries, built a road to the coast and ruled a large following of Oorlam, Nama and dependent Herero. His power rested on firearms and alliances rather than on a fixed territory.
orlam-afrikaner-state.e: After Jonker's death in 1861 and his son Christian's death in battle at Otjimbingwe in 1863, the Herero under Maharero won their independence. Jan Jonker Afrikaner was finally defeated by the Herero in 1880, and the group lost its land.

olbia.t: Milesian colony on the Bug-Dnieper estuary that was the main Greek gateway to the Scythians, described first-hand by Herodotus.
olbia.o: Greeks from Miletus first settled on Berezan island in the 7th century BCE, and around 550 BCE founded Olbia ('the prosperous') on the right bank of the Hypanis (Southern Bug) estuary. Its people also called it Borysthenes, after the Dnieper. The colony took over much of the fertile surrounding steppe edge.
olbia.r: Olbia traded wine, olive oil and fine pottery to the Scythians for grain, fish, hides and slaves, and lived alongside Scythian rulers, one of whom, Scyles, kept a house there. A self-governing polis, it worshipped Apollo Delphinios and Achilles, and issued early cast bronze money shaped like dolphins. Herodotus visited in the 5th century BCE.
olbia.e: Olbia resisted a siege by Alexander's general Zopyrion c. 331 BCE but declined in the later Hellenistic period. Around 55 BCE the Getae under Burebista sacked it. It was later rebuilt on a smaller scale under Roman protection and abandoned in the 4th century CE. The ruins near Parutyne in Ukraine are a protected reserve.

orchomenus-boeotia.t: Ancient Boeotian city, heir of Mycenaean Orchomenos, which rivalled Thebes for leadership of Boeotia until the Thebans destroyed it in 364 BCE.
orchomenus-boeotia.o: After the collapse of the Mycenaean Kingdom of Orchomenos c. 1200 BCE, the town survived beside the refilled Lake Copais. In the Iron Age it became a Boeotian polis and the main rival of Thebes, sometimes leading western Boeotia. Its cult of the Graces, the Charites, was among the oldest in Greece.
orchomenus-boeotia.r: Orchomenus was a member of the Boeotian League and an oligarchy of landowners. It sided with Sparta against Thebes in the early 4th century BCE and fought at Coronea in 394 BCE. Its festival of the Charitesia attracted poets and musicians, and Pindar wrote an ode for an Orchomenian victor.
orchomenus-boeotia.e: Thebes destroyed Orchomenus in 364 BCE, killing its men. Philip II rebuilt it after Chaeronea in 338 BCE. Sulla defeated Mithridates's army nearby in 85 BCE, and the town, under Rome from 146 BCE, continued on a smaller scale.
orchomenus-boeotia.re: Greek religion; cult of the Charites

omagua.t: A powerful riverine chiefdom on the upper Amazon whose dense villages amazed the first Spanish explorers in the 16th century.
omagua.o: The Omagua, a Tupi-Guarani-speaking people, settled along the Amazon, known locally as the Solimões, and its islands between the Napo and Juruá rivers. Their expansion along the river is dated archaeologically to around 1000.
omagua.r: Gaspar de Carvajal, who accompanied Francisco de Orellana's voyage down the Amazon in 1542, described the territory of a chief called Machiparo and densely populated villages lining the riverbanks. The Omagua farmed manioc and maize on the fertile floodplain, kept turtles in pens and traded goods along the river. They flattened the foreheads of infants as a mark of status. They were noted for fine painted pottery and cotton cloth.
omagua.e: Slave raids from Portuguese Brazil, epidemics and the missions of the Jesuit Samuel Fritz around 1700 broke up the chiefdom. Survivors moved upriver into Spanish territory, settling around San Joaquín de Omaguas in Peru. A few communities, also known as Cambeba, survive in Peru and Brazil.

old-swiss-confederacy.t: The loose alliance of Alpine cantons that grew from a 1291 pact into a neutral federation of thirteen members, the forerunner of modern Switzerland.
old-swiss-confederacy.o: Tradition dates the Confederacy to the Federal Charter of August 1291, a defensive pact between Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden against outside lords, above all the Habsburgs. Victories at Morgarten in 1315, Sempach in 1386 and Näfels in 1388 drew in Lucerne, Zürich, Glarus, Zug and Bern, and by 1513 the alliance numbered thirteen cantons.
old-swiss-confederacy.r: There was no central government. The cantons, a mix of rural assemblies and patrician city republics, sent envoys to the Diet (Tagsatzung), which decided only by consensus. They jointly ruled subject territories and kept associates such as the Three Leagues and the Republic of Geneva. Swiss pikemen were Europe's most sought-after mercenaries, and the Reformation split the cantons into Catholic and Reformed camps that fought several civil wars.
old-swiss-confederacy.e: Independence from the Holy Roman Empire was recognised at the Peace of Westphalia in 1648. In 1798 French armies invaded and replaced the old order with the centralised Helvetic Republic. Napoleon's Act of Mediation of 1803 restored a federation, from which the modern Swiss state developed.

oxybii.t: Ligurian people of the coast near Fréjus who, with the Deciates, provoked Rome's first intervention beyond the Alps in 154 BCE.
oxybii.o: Known chiefly from Polybius, the Oxybii lived on the coast west of Antibes, near the port of Aegitna, probably around modern Mandelieu or Cannes.
oxybii.r: Nothing is recorded of their rulers. Polybius tells that they attacked Roman envoys landing at Aegitna and wounded one of them.
oxybii.e: In 154 BCE the consul Quintus Opimius marched against them, took Aegitna and defeated them and the Deciates. Their land was given to Massalia and later absorbed into Gallia Narbonensis, where the Roman colony of Forum Julii (Fréjus) was founded nearby.

ober-ost.t: German military state in occupied Lithuania, Courland and western Belarus during the First World War, run by Hindenburg and Ludendorff's staff.
ober-ost.o: After the German offensives of 1915 drove Russian armies out of Courland, Lithuania and the Grodno-Białystok region, the territory was placed under the Supreme Commander in the East, Oberbefehlshaber Ost, Paul von Hindenburg, with Erich Ludendorff as chief of staff. The headquarters moved to Kovno (Kaunas).
ober-ost.r: Ober Ost was a military administration that tried to remake the land according to German plans: it requisitioned food, timber and livestock, imposed forced labour and controlled movement through passes. It also sponsored newspapers, schools and surveys among Lithuanians, Latvians, Poles, Jews and Belarusians, seeing the region as a German colony.
ober-ost.e: After the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk in March 1918, Germany allowed client institutions, including the Lithuanian Taryba, which had declared independence in February 1918, and planned a Duchy of Courland and Semigallia (1918). Germany's defeat in November 1918 ended the administration, and the Republic of Lithuania and Republic of Latvia emerged.
ober-ost.re: Lutheran and Catholic Christianity, Judaism, Orthodoxy

olynthus.t: Chief city of Chalcidice, head of the Chalcidian League, whose destruction by Philip II in 348 BCE left the best-preserved classical Greek town plan.
olynthus.o: Olynthus stood on hills near the head of the Toronaic Gulf. It was a town of the Bottiaeans until 479 BCE, when the Persian commander Artabazus massacred its people and handed it to Chalcidian Greeks under Critobulus of Torone. In 432 BCE many Chalcidians abandoned their coastal towns to settle there, at the urging of Perdiccas II of Macedon.
olynthus.r: Olynthus became the centre of the Chalcidian League, a federal state with shared citizenship and coinage of fine silver. A new town on a regular grid of blocks was built on the North Hill; excavations led by David Robinson in the 1920s and 1930s uncovered whole houses with courtyards, mosaics and household goods, a rich picture of daily life.
olynthus.e: Sparta forced the league to submit after a war in 382-379 BCE. Restored, Olynthus became Philip II's main rival in the north. Despite Demosthenes' Olynthiac speeches urging Athenian help, Philip took the city by treachery in 348 BCE, razed it and sold its people into slavery.

orange-river-colony.t: The British colony that replaced the Orange Free State after the Second Boer War, until it joined the Union of South Africa.
orange-river-colony.o: British forces took Bloemfontein in March 1900, and Britain proclaimed the annexation of the Orange Free State as the Orange River Colony in May 1900. Boer commandos fought on until the Treaty of Vereeniging in May 1902, when British rule became effective.
orange-river-colony.r: During the war, farms were burned and Boer women and children held in concentration camps, where thousands died, as did many black Africans in separate camps. Under Lord Milner's reconstruction the colony was run by appointed officials. After the Liberal victory in Britain, responsible government was granted in 1907, and the Orangia Unie party under Abraham Fischer took office.
orange-river-colony.e: In 1910 the colony joined the Union of South Africa as the Orange Free State Province, keeping Bloemfontein as the seat of the Appellate Division, which made it the country's judicial capital.

ordovices.t: Mountain peoples of north-west Wales who hosted Caratacus' last stand and fought Rome until Agricola crushed them in 77 or 78.
ordovices.o: The Ordovices held the uplands of Snowdonia and much of mid and north Wales, a region of small hillforts, stone-walled roundhouses and pastoral farming. They enter written history through Tacitus, who records that the British leader Caratacus moved his war against Rome into their territory around 51 after leaving the Silures.
ordovices.r: No coins, kings or towns are known, and power was probably held by local chiefs controlling upland grazing and fortified settlements. Anglesey, the island of Mona, lay on their borders and was a centre of the druids, whose sanctuary Suetonius Paulinus attacked in 60 before Boudica's revolt recalled him. Their resistance made the region one of the last parts of Wales to be pacified.
ordovices.e: Around 77 the Ordovices destroyed a Roman cavalry unit. The new governor Agricola answered with a campaign that, Tacitus says, nearly wiped out the people, and then seized Anglesey. Their land was held by forts such as Segontium at Caernarfon, and no civitas of the Ordovices is known in Roman Britain.

orange-river-sovereignty.t: Britain's brief attempt to rule the land between the Orange and Vaal rivers, abandoned in 1854 in favour of the Orange Free State.
orange-river-sovereignty.o: Sir Harry Smith proclaimed British sovereignty over the territory between the Orange and Vaal rivers in February 1848, hoping to control the Boers and keep peace with the Griqua and Basotho. Andries Pretorius rose against the annexation but was defeated at Boomplaats in August 1848.
orange-river-sovereignty.r: A British Resident, Major Henry Warden, governed from Bloemfontein with little money and few troops. His boundary lines between Boer farms and the lands of Moshoeshoe's Basotho Kingdom satisfied no one, and British forces were defeated at Viervoet in 1851 and fought an indecisive battle at Berea in 1852. Boer farmers resented taxes and the lack of protection.
orange-river-sovereignty.e: London decided the territory was not worth its cost. By the Bloemfontein Convention of 23 February 1854 Britain withdrew, and the burghers formed the Orange Free State, which kept Bloemfontein as its capital.
orange-river-sovereignty.re: Dutch Reformed Christianity, Sotho traditional religion

obotrite-confederation.t: A union of Slavic tribes in Mecklenburg whose princes alternated between alliance and war with Franks, Danes and Saxons, founding Mecklenburg's ruling house.
obotrite-confederation.o: The Obotrites (Abodrites) were West Slavic tribes who settled the coastlands of Mecklenburg and Holstein from the 7th century. From around 780 they appear as allies of Charlemagne against the Saxons, and their prince Drasco helped defeat the Nordalbingian Saxons in 798.
obotrite-confederation.r: The confederation united several tribes, including the Wagrians and Polabians, under princes with strongholds such as Mecklenburg near Wismar and Starigard (Oldenburg in Holstein). Trade passed through the port of Reric until the Danish king Godfred destroyed it in 808. Princes Gottschalk and Henry tried to Christianise the realm; a pagan revolt in 1066 killed Gottschalk.
obotrite-confederation.e: The Wendish Crusade of 1147 and the campaigns of Henry the Lion broke Obotrite power; Prince Niklot was killed in 1160. His son Pribislav accepted Saxon overlordship and Christianity in 1167, founding the Lordship of Mecklenburg, whose dynasty ruled until 1918.

ottoman-egypt.t: Egypt as an Ottoman province for nearly three centuries, ruled by pashas from Istanbul while the old Mamluk elite kept real power.
ottoman-egypt.o: Sultan Selim I destroyed the Mamluk Sultanate at Marj Dabiq in 1516 and Ridaniya in January 1517, then hanged the last Mamluk sultan Tumanbay at Cairo. Egypt became a province of the Ottoman Empire, governed under the law code issued by Suleiman's grand vizier Ibrahim Pasha in 1525.
ottoman-egypt.r: A pasha appointed from Istanbul governed with regiments such as the Janissaries, but Mamluk households re-emerged as beys holding key offices. Egypt supplied grain and tax revenue to Istanbul and controlled the coffee and spice trade of the Red Sea. Al-Azhar remained the leading centre of Sunni learning. In 1768 Ali Bey al-Kabir briefly declared independence.
ottoman-egypt.e: Bonaparte's invasion in 1798 and the French occupation of Egypt shattered Mamluk power. In the turmoil after the French left, Muhammad Ali was recognised as governor in 1805, beginning Egypt under Muhammad Ali.

odrysian-kingdom.t: The strongest Thracian state, a kingdom stretching from the Aegean to the Danube whose rich tombs and Greek-style city of Seuthopolis survive in Bulgaria.
odrysian-kingdom.o: Around 480 BCE, after the Persian retreat from Europe, Teres I united Thracian tribes of the Hebrus (Maritsa) valley under the Odrysians. His son Sitalces extended rule from Abdera on the Aegean to the Danube and allied with Athens at the start of the Peloponnesian War.
odrysian-kingdom.r: The king ruled through relatives and tribal princes, drawing tribute from Thracian tribes and Greek coastal cities; Thucydides valued the yearly income at some 400 talents. Gold and silver vessels such as the Panagyurishte and Rogozen treasures show elite wealth. Cotys I strengthened the crown in the 4th century, and Seuthes III built Seuthopolis near Kazanlak, where painted tombs survive.
odrysian-kingdom.e: Philip II of Macedon conquered much of the kingdom after 342 BCE. Odrysian rulers revived under Macedonian and then Roman overlordship as client kings. In 46 CE, after the murder of Rhoemetalces III, Claudius annexed the realm as the province of Thrace.

omani-empire.t: The Al Bu Said maritime empire of Muscat and Zanzibar, which dominated the Swahili coast and the trade of the western Indian Ocean.
omani-empire.o: In the 1740s Ahmad ibn Said, governor of Sohar, expelled the Persian forces that had intervened in the civil war of the Ya'aruba dynasty and was elected imam. His family, the Al Bu Said, took the title of sayyid and later sultan and made Muscat their capital.
omani-empire.r: Oman's fleets and merchants controlled trade between Arabia, Persia, India and East Africa. Gwadar on the Makran coast was acquired in the 1780s and Bandar Abbas leased from Persia. Said ibn Sultan, ruling from 1806 to 1856, built up Zanzibar, planting cloves and promoting the caravan trade in ivory and slaves, and moved his residence there around 1840. Treaties were signed with Britain, the United States and France.
omani-empire.e: When Said died in 1856 his sons disputed the succession. In 1861 the British-arbitrated Canning Award divided the realm into the Sultanate of Zanzibar and the Sultanate of Muscat and Oman.

ottoman-tripolitania.t: Tripoli as an Ottoman province and corsair base, ruled by pashas and then deys until the Karamanli dynasty took power in 1711.
ottoman-tripolitania.o: The Ottoman fleet captured Tripoli from the Knights Hospitaller in 1551. The corsair Turgut Reis, who had helped take the city, became its governor in 1553 and extended Ottoman authority along the coast and inland, making Tripolitania a province of the Ottoman Empire.
ottoman-tripolitania.r: Pashas sent from Istanbul shared power with Janissary officers and, from the early 17th century, deys chosen by the garrison. Corsairing in the Mediterranean and the trans-Saharan slave trade sustained the treasury, and the Sultanate of Fezzan paid tribute. Dey Mehmed Saqizli extended control over Cyrenaica in the 1630s and 1640s.
ottoman-tripolitania.e: Chronic coups between Janissaries and pashas ended in 1711, when the cavalry officer Ahmed Karamanli seized power, killed the Ottoman officials and founded a hereditary dynasty, beginning Karamanli Tripoli.

ogedeid-khanate.t: The Central Asian realm of Ögedei's descendants, whose leader Kaidu waged a forty-year war against Kublai Khan.
ogedeid-khanate.o: Genghis Khan gave his third son Ögedei pastures in the region of the Emil and the upper Irtysh in Dzungaria. Ögedei became Great Khan in 1229, and his line ruled the appanage. After the throne passed to the Toluids in 1251 they were purged, but Ögedei's grandson Kaidu rebuilt their power from the 1260s.
ogedeid-khanate.r: Kaidu ruled from the Ili and Talas valleys, dominating the Chagatai Khanate through his ally Duwa and challenging Kublai Khan's claim to be Great Khan. The khanate was a nomadic military power that drew revenue from the oasis towns of Transoxiana and the Tarim, administered by officials such as Mas'ud Beg.
ogedeid-khanate.e: Kaidu died in 1301 after battle against Yuan forces. His son Chapar made peace with the Yuan in 1304, but Duwa turned on him, and by 1310 the Chagatai Khanate had absorbed the Ogedeid lands.

odessa-soviet-republic.t: A Bolshevik republic proclaimed in Odessa in January 1918, which lasted only until the German and Austrian advance in March.
odessa-soviet-republic.o: In January 1918 Bolsheviks and their allies seized Odessa after street fighting with forces of the Ukrainian People's Republic. They proclaimed the Odessa Soviet Republic, with Vladimir Yudovsky as head of its council of people's commissars, claiming authority over the city and surrounding province.
odessa-soviet-republic.r: The republic relied on Red Guards and Black Sea Fleet sailors, imposed levies on the wealthy and carried out arrests and executions. It also fought the Kingdom of Romania, which had occupied Bessarabia, and reached a short-lived ceasefire agreement with it. Its control barely extended beyond the city.
odessa-soviet-republic.e: After the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk, Austro-Hungarian and German troops advanced on Odessa, and the Soviet leaders evacuated the city in March 1918. The republic was nominally merged into the Ukrainian Soviet Republic and ceased to exist.

orungu-kingdom.t: A Myene-speaking kingdom of the Ogooue delta in Gabon that controlled the slave and later the rubber trade at Cape Lopez.
orungu-kingdom.o: The Orungu established a kingdom around the Ogooue delta and Cape Lopez by the early 18th century, displacing earlier inhabitants. Their position at the mouth of Gabon's largest river gave them control of trade between the interior and European ships.
orungu-kingdom.r: The Orungu king, with a council of clan heads, monopolised trade with Europeans at Cape Lopez, acting as a middleman for slaves supplied from up the Ogooue. In the 19th century Cape Lopez became an outlet for an illegal slave trade to Brazil and Cuba, later replaced by trade in ivory, ebony and rubber.
orungu-kingdom.e: French influence grew after the 1860s, and the area was absorbed into French Gabon. The kingship declined into a local chieftaincy, which the French ceased to recognise by the late 1920s.

oretani.t: An Iberian people of the upper Guadalquivir whose city Castulo controlled the silver mines of the Sierra Morena and gave Hannibal his wife.
oretani.o: The Oretani lived in the upper Guadalquivir valley and the southern Meseta, in modern Jaén and Ciudad Real, from the mid-first millennium BCE. They took their name from the town of Oretum, but their leading city was Castulo near Linares, a crossroads between the coast and the interior.
oretani.r: Their wealth came from the silver and lead mines of the Sierra Morena, exploited intensively under Carthaginian and then Roman control. Castulo had rich princely tombs and later minted bronze coins with an Iberian legend. Hannibal married Himilce, said to be a princess of Castulo, tying the Oretani to Barcid Iberia.
oretani.e: In 206 BCE Castulo went over to Rome during the Scipionic campaigns. The Oretani joined the revolt of 197 BCE but were absorbed into Hispania Citerior and later Tarraconensis, and Castulo remained an important Roman mining town.

oriental-republic-of-uruguay.t: The small republic between Argentina and Brazil, created as a buffer state in 1828, which built one of the earliest welfare states in the Americas.
oriental-republic-of-uruguay.o: The Preliminary Peace Convention of 1828, mediated by Britain, ended the Cisplatine War between Brazil and the United Provinces of the Río de la Plata and made the former Cisplatina an independent state. Its first constitution was sworn on 18 July 1830, and Fructuoso Rivera became the first president.
oriental-republic-of-uruguay.r: Politics were long dominated by two parties, the Blancos and Colorados, whose rivalry led to the Guerra Grande of 1839 to 1851, with a nine-year siege of Montevideo. Immigration from Spain and Italy and exports of beef and wool brought prosperity. José Batlle y Ordóñez, president in the early 20th century, introduced social welfare, secular education and the eight-hour day. Political violence involving the Tupamaros guerrillas preceded a military dictatorship from 1973 to 1985.
oriental-republic-of-uruguay.e: Democracy returned in 1985, and the left-wing Frente Amplio governed from 2005 to 2020 under Tabaré Vázquez and José Mujica, legalising cannabis in 2013. Uruguay ranks among Latin America's most stable democracies.

ozolian-locris.t: Confederation of the western Locrians on the Gulf of Corinth, centred on Amphissa, whose clash with the Amphictyony brought Philip II into central Greece.
ozolian-locris.o: The western or Ozolian Locrians lived on the northern shore of the Gulf of Corinth, west of Delphi, in small hill towns such as Amphissa, Chaleion and Oeanthea. They were related to the Locrians of Opuntian Locris but separated by Phocis and Doris. Naupactus was theirs until Athens gave it to Messenian refugees c. 456 BCE.
ozolian-locris.r: Thucydides described the western Locrians as still carrying arms in daily life, a sign of archaic customs. Their towns were loosely confederated, with Amphissa the most important. A bronze tablet from Chaleion of the 5th century BCE regulates disputes between towns, a rare early example of Greek inter-state law.
ozolian-locris.e: When Amphissa farmed the sacred plain of Delphi, the Amphictyony declared the Fourth Sacred War; Philip II destroyed Amphissa in 338 BCE. Western Locris later joined the Aetolian League and came under Rome in 146 BCE.

osismii.t: Gallic people of the far western tip of Brittany, the end of the known world for Greek and Roman geographers.
osismii.o: The Osismii lived in Finistère and western Côtes-d'Armor. The Greek explorer Pytheas probably referred to them as the Ostimioi around 320 BCE, placing them on a promontory facing the Ocean. Caesar lists them among the Armorican peoples.
osismii.r: Their economy rested on farming, fishing and sea trade along the Atlantic route to Britain. No ruler or central town is recorded before the conquest.
osismii.e: They submitted to Publius Crassus in 57 BCE and supported the Veneti in 56 BCE. Under Rome their capital was Vorgium (Carhaix). In late antiquity their land was settled by migrants from Britain and became part of Domnonée and Cornouaille.

organisation-of-western-continental-gree.t: Regional revolutionary government of western mainland Greece in 1821-1822, organised by Alexandros Mavrokordatos at Missolonghi.
organisation-of-western-continental-gree.o: Western mainland Greece, from the Gulf of Corinth to Epirus, rose against the Ottomans in the spring of 1821. In November 1821 the Phanariot politician Alexandros Mavrokordatos gathered local representatives at Missolonghi, where they adopted a charter and created a senate to govern the region and coordinate the military chieftains.
organisation-of-western-continental-gree.r: The organisation had a senate of local notables and military leaders, with Mavrokordatos as president. It raised revenue, supplied armed bands and tried to restrain the chieftains, many of whom had served as armatoloi under the Ottomans. Missolonghi, a lagoon town, became the region's centre and later the scene of famous sieges.
organisation-of-western-continental-gree.e: With the First National Assembly at Epidaurus in January 1822 and the founding of the First Hellenic Republic, regional bodies were placed under the central government and were abolished during 1822. Mavrokordatos became president of the national executive.

ostrogothic-kingdom.t: Gothic kingdom of Theodoric the Great in Italy, which preserved Roman government and culture before Justinian's armies destroyed it.
ostrogothic-kingdom.o: The Ostrogoths, settled in the Balkans as federates of the eastern empire, were sent to Italy by the emperor Zeno under their king Theodoric. They invaded in 489, besieged Odoacer in Ravenna and killed him in 493, and Theodoric became ruler of Italy under nominal imperial authority.
ostrogothic-kingdom.r: Theodoric governed through Roman officials and the Senate, while the Goths formed the army and kept their Arian faith. Romans such as Cassiodorus and Boethius served him, though he executed Boethius in 524. Ravenna gained Sant'Apollinare Nuovo and his mausoleum. His realm reached into Provence, Dalmatia and the Alps, and he led a network of Germanic kingdoms through marriage alliances.
ostrogothic-kingdom.e: After Theodoric's death in 526, the murder of his daughter Amalasuntha gave Justinian a pretext to invade in 535. Belisarius and Narses fought the Goths for almost twenty years, leaving Italy devastated. Totila was killed at Busta Gallorum in 552, and Teia at Mons Lactarius in 552 or 553.

onogurs.t: Oghur Turkic nomads of the Pontic steppe whose name survives in the word 'Hungary', and from whom the Bulgars of Kubrat emerged.
onogurs.o: The Onogurs, meaning 'ten Oghurs', are first recorded in 463 when, with the Saragurs and Urogs, they sent envoys to Constantinople after being driven west by the Sabirs. They settled in the steppe between the Kuban, the Sea of Azov and the lower Don, in contact with the Caucasus and Byzantine Crimea.
onogurs.r: They were a tribal confederation of pastoral nomads organised into ten tribes under chieftains. Byzantine writers record their dealings with Constantinople and their conversion attempts; their leader Organa and his nephew Kubrat had ties to the Byzantine court. In the late 6th century they came under the Western Turkic Khaganate, alongside the Utigurs and Kutrigurs.
onogurs.e: Around 632 Kubrat threw off Turkic rule and united Onogurs, Utigurs and Kutrigurs as Old Great Bulgaria. After his death the Khazars scattered it, and his sons led groups to the Danube and Volga. The Onogur name, through Slavic and Latin, gave Europe its name for the Hungarians.

orchomenus-arcadia.t: Ancient hill city of northern Arcadia, a rival of Mantinea that refused to join the Arcadian League.
orchomenus-arcadia.o: Orchomenus occupied a hill between two upland plains in northern Arcadia. Tradition made it the seat of early Arcadian kings; the last, Aristocrates, was said to have been stoned for betraying the Messenians to Sparta in the 7th century BCE. Homer called it 'rich in flocks'.
orchomenus-arcadia.r: Orchomenus was an ally of Sparta in the Peloponnesian League and a rival of Mantinea, with which it fought over land and leadership in Arcadia. It sent troops to Thermopylae and Plataea. In 370 BCE it refused to join the new Arcadian League dominated by Mantinea and Tegea.
orchomenus-arcadia.e: In the Hellenistic period Orchomenus was taken in turn by the Aetolian League, Sparta and the Achaean League, and Antigonus Doson of the Antigonid Kingdom of Macedonia captured it in 223 BCE. It passed under Rome in 146 BCE.

olcades.t: A people of the southern Meseta whose capital Althaia was Hannibal's first conquest as commander in Iberia, in 221 BCE.
olcades.o: The Olcades lived in the upper Guadiana and Júcar region of the southern Meseta, probably in modern Cuenca and Ciudad Real. Their origins are obscure, and ancient sources mention them only in connection with the Carthaginian campaigns.
olcades.r: Nothing is known of their institutions beyond their capital, which Polybius calls Althaia and Livy Cartala, and their wealth in cattle and grain.
olcades.e: In 221 BCE Hannibal attacked them, took Althaia and forced them to pay tribute. The next year Olcadian refugees joined the Carpetani and Vaccaei against him at the Tagus and were defeated. They vanish from the record after this, absorbed into Barcid Iberia and later Roman Hispania.

occupied-enemy-territory-administration.t: The British-led military government of the former Ottoman Levant after the First World War, which preceded the French and British mandates.
occupied-enemy-territory-administration.o: After General Allenby's forces took Jerusalem in December 1917 and conquered the rest of the Levant in 1918, the occupied Ottoman territories were placed under military administration as Occupied Enemy Territory, as international law required until a peace settlement.
occupied-enemy-territory-administration.r: The territory was divided into zones: OETA South, roughly Palestine, under British officers; OETA East, inland Syria and Transjordan, administered by Faisal's Arab government; and OETA North (or West), the coast, under French officers. The administration preserved Ottoman law, restored supplies after wartime famine and began reconstruction. Ronald Storrs served as military governor of Jerusalem.
occupied-enemy-territory-administration.e: In 1920 the San Remo conference assigned mandates to Britain and France. OETA South was replaced by a civil administration under Herbert Samuel in July 1920, forming Mandatory Palestine, while France occupied inland Syria after defeating the Arab Kingdom of Syria.
